articles.title: AI chip boom pushes Samsung profits to record $80bn
articles.summary: The tech giant is also expected to get a boost from its latest folding devices that were launched in August.
articles.body:
Samsung Electronics says it expects a nine-fold surge in its quarterly profits compared with a year earlier, driven by surging demand for memory chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) data centres.

The tech giant estimates that its operating profit for the three months to the end of September will jump to 107.4tn won (£61bn; $80bn), its fourth quarter in a row of record earnings.

Samsung is one of the world's largest memory chip makers alongside local rival SK Hynix and Micron in the US, which produce chips crucial for AI firms like Nvidia.

Samsung, which makes the Galaxy Fold and S26 smartphones, is also expected to get a boost from its latest folding devices that were launched in August.

The firm's full third-quarter earnings will be published at the end of October.

Some of South Korea's biggest companies release previews of their earnings to advise investors ahead of more detailed reports.

These forecasts are treated with much more credibility than estimates by external analysts as they are backed by internal company data.

There has been huge global demand for computer chips that power AI development, helping to lift the earnings and shares of manufacturers linked to the technology.

The surge in demand in recent years has resulted in a shortage of semiconductors globally, pushing up sales for firms like Samsung, with its stock market valuation crossing $1tn (£757bn) earlier this year .

Investment in the industry has surged, with US tech giants including Google, Amazon and Meta pledging to pour more than $650bn into AI projects this year.

In June, South Korea unveiled plans for at least $880bn in projects led by Samsung and SK Hynix to build out the country's chip manufacturing capabilities in the coming years.

Rival Asian firms in Japan, China and Taiwan are also investing heavily in chip plants as demand for AI soars.

A chip shortage driven by surging demand has led firms including Samsung to raise prices, making products such as smartphones and computers more expensive.

articles.title: HubSpot, one of the UK's biggest technology companies, is cutting hundreds of jobs; CEO in 'layoff email' to employees: I want to make it clear that ...
articles.summary: One of the United Kingdom's (UK) biggest technology companies, HubSpot, is cutting hundreds of jobs.
articles.body: One of the United Kingdom's (UK) biggest technology companies, HubSpot, is cutting hundreds of jobs. To be precise, Cambridge-based CRM software company HubSpot is laying off 660 employees, which is 7% of its workforce. In an email to employees, HubSpot CEO Yamini Rangan called the job cuts as a restructuring and the company taking an AI strategy shift while insisting that the cuts are not driven by AI efficiencies. The company's SEC filing says that the job cuts timeline depends on local consultation law, which in Ireland means a statutory 30-day minimum and criminal penalties for ignoring it.HubSpot board authorised the plan on October 1 and CEO Rangan told employees this week (October 6), according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The company reaffirmed its revenue guidance the same day. CEO Rangan termed layoffs as part of a broader change in how HubSpot operates rather than a straightforward cost-cutting exercise. The company shared the layoff memo sent to employees in its 8-K filing with the SEC.Read HobSpot CEO Yamini Rangan's 'layoff email' to employeesTeam,I am writing to share some very difficult news. We have decided to reduce the size of our team by ~7% and will be saying goodbye to nearly 660 HubSpotters. We did not make this decision lightly and approached it with the seriousness and care it deserves.If you are one of the employees impacted in the U.S., you will get an email within the next 15 minutes with information and support. In other countries, this process will vary based on local laws and practices.Why are we taking this stepOver the past year, we have shifted our strategy from building software that helps customers grow to delivering outcomes for them with AI. That shift is transforming product, pricing and how we serve our customers. But we also need to fundamentally change the way we are organized to compete and win.We need to move faster, stay closer to our customers and focus our resources on our highest priorities to set ourselves up for success in this next chapter. That requires difficult choices about how we are organized.What are we changingWe are making three changes to how we operate:1. Organize around customer outcomes. Customers don’t think in Hubs and features. They want to generate demand, win deals, delight customers, and scale growth. We will organize product teams around these outcomes instead of hubs, with each team owning the full customer journey and clear accountability for the outcome. As a product focused company, our team of builders are key to driving transformation. We have always worked hard to be the best product company for GTM teams in the world, and the changes we are making will help ensure that remains true going forward, as we adapt to the new way to build and deliver outcomes.2. Build a flatter organization with fewer layers. We will reduce management layers and move decisions closer to the people doing the work. We will simplify the organization so decisions can be made faster.3. Create agile teams with clear ownership. Teams need the context, capabilities, and authority to get work done. We will reduce fragmented ownership so teams can make decisions and execute with speed and clarity.What is this not aboutI also want to be clear about what is not driving this decision.This is not driven by AI-related efficiencies. We believe in a world where AI helps make us more productive and we will continue to invest to make that happen. This change is about aligning our organization with our strategy and how we need to operate going forward.This is not simply a cost-cutting exercise. We have been thoughtful about how we invest in AI while balancing growth and profitability. We have been disciplined about growing headcount slower than revenue, and we will continue to do so. This change is about where and how we invest so we can put more resources behind our biggest opportunities.None of that makes today easier. We are saying goodbye to colleagues who have helped build HubSpot. We owe them our gratitude, our respect, and our support through this transition.What principles guided usIt was very important to me, our executive team, and our founders that we had a clear set of principles to guide the process. We defined the structure, roles, and capabilities needed to execute our strategy. We then assessed every role against the same six criteria. The reduction was the outcome of that work, not the starting point.• Strategic need: Is this role critical to delivering our strategy, priorities, and outcomes?• Layers and spans: Do we have the right number of layers and spans to move quickly?• Drive revenue: Are we protecting our capacity to generate demand and drive revenue?• Capability: Are we investing in the capabilities we need?• Capacity: Is the role needed at the scale required?• Leadership: Do we have the right leaders for the next phase, in the right roles?Supporting employees who are leavingWe are committed to ensuring every employee leaving HubSpot has a dignified, well-supported experience. To take care of these teammates, we looked at severance, benefits, career support and transition support and have done our best to be thoughtful and fair. The transition support will vary by region based on global requirements, but will generally include the following:• Severance: 20 weeks of base pay + 1 week per year of service, up to 30 weeks• Health benefits: US: COBRA (5 months as a lump sum); Global: Modern Health (5 months)• Career support: Everyone will have access to six months of career transition outplacement services to help with their job search.• Laptops and WFH set-up: Impacted employees may keep their HubSpot laptops (it will be cleaned of any company data remotely), as well as any work from home gear like monitors and keyboards.• Connect conversations: All US departing employees will have the opportunity for a 1:1 conversation today with a HubSpot manager. Invites will be sent shortly.What happens nextToday, our priority is taking care of the HubSpotters who are leaving and giving everyone clarity as quickly as we can. If you are in the U.S. and your role is impacted, you will receive an email from the People Team within the next 15 minutes with details about your transition and the support available to you. Outside the U.S., impacted employees will also hear from us within the next 15 minutes about what happens next. The process and timing will differ by country based on local requirements.Every departing HubSpotter will also have the opportunity to speak 1:1 with a HubSpot Manager within the next day. We know an email cannot answer every question, and we want you to have a person to talk to. If you are in the U.S. and your role is not impacted, you will receive confirmation from the People team within the next 15 minutes.Closing thoughtsTo HubSpotters leaving us: I am deeply sorry. I know this decision affects far more than your job. It affects you, your family, your plans, and people you have worked alongside for years. Your work here mattered and thank you for what you have given to HubSpot and to each other. I am deeply grateful.For those staying, you are saying goodbye to friends, managers, teammates, and people you care about. Please make space for that and support each other. Next week, we will spend time together talking about the organization we are building and what comes next.YaminiYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles off north coast of Qatar, UKMTO says
articles.summary: The UK maritime agency has reported a rise in attacks on vessels in the vital Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body:
A number of casualties have been reported after a tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar was struck by multiple projectiles, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency has announced.

The vessel was hit by several projectiles 94 kilometres (58 miles) north of Madinat ash Shamal, UKMTO said on Wednesday. The incident comes as the British maritime agency reported a recent rise in attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

UKMTO did not say how many people were killed or injured in this latest attack, adding that authorities were investigating. It did not specify the origin of the ship.

An attack on a vessel in the middle of the Gulf is unusual. The Maritime Executive, a publication specialising in commercial shipping, said it was the first reported attack on a tanker in the western half of the Gulf in weeks.

Qatar has not commented on the reported attack, which falls within its exclusive economic zone.

Vessels have more commonly been targeted in the strategically important Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway linking the Gulf with the Gulf of Oman.

Before the United States-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, the strait typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day, and shipments through it accounted for about 20 percent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies.

In retaliation for US-Israeli attacks, Iran effectively closed the strait, while Washington has maintained a blockade on Iranian ports.

UKMTO said on Tuesday that there had been nine attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz this month, representing half of the September total in the waterway and the Gulf combined.

Despite the attacks, oil exports from the Middle East have risen to, and according to provisional data even surpassed , pre-war levels in recent weeks.

The seven-day moving average of Middle East crude exports reached 18.3 million barrels per day (bpd) on September 30, compared with about 18 million bpd on average in the 12 months before the war, according to Kpler, a data firm.

articles.title: US bars Fiji-based man over corruption tied to China
articles.summary: The State Department has accused the man of paying bribes to Fijian citizens to advance Chinese interests.
articles.body:
The US Department of State has publicly designated a Fiji-based man for his involvement in corruption on behalf of Chinese actors.

Zhao Fugang, the director of the Overseas Chinese Service Center, “abused his public position by paying bribes to Fijian citizens to advance China-based government, business, and criminal interests”, the State Department said in a press release on Wednesday.

“His actions constituted significant corruption and adversely affected U.S. interests in Fiji.”

The designation renders Zhao and his immediate family members “generally ineligible for entry into the United States”.

The US embassy in Suva, Fiji’s capital, said Zhao’s actions left the Pacific nation open to “malign foreign influence facilitated by Chinese government, business, and criminal actors”.

The embassy also said, “Public reporting shows an established trend of criminals operating across the Pacific with ties to China.”

Beijing says Overseas Chinese Service Centers help its nationals with administrative issues abroad, such as renewing driving licences. However, rights groups have alleged they are fronts for Beijing to push interests abroad, including the targeting of dissidents.

In February, the Trump administration sanctioned two leaders of Pacific island nations for alleged corruption tied to China. The US Department of State issued a notice alleging that Hokkons Baules, the president of Palau’s Senate, and Anderson Jibas, a former mayor in the Marshall Islands, had created openings for China to increase its influence in the region.

articles.title: Three people killed in attacks on Saudi Arabia airports, officials say
articles.summary: The Houthis have claimed responsibility for the attacks, which mark an escalation in the conflict.
articles.body:
Three people have been killed in attacks on Saudi Arabia airports over two days, authorities said, as flare-up of fighting spilled across the Yemen border into the kingdom.

Two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack at Abha International Airport, Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation (Gaca) said in a statement on Wednesday.

In a separate incident, one person was killed and eight were wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital, it added.

The attacks, which the Houthis have claimed responsibility for, mark an escalation in the renewed war between the Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

The two airports were attacked on 6 and 7 October, according to Gaca, which did not specify when each airport was hit.

Two women, of Moroccan and Algerian nationalities, were killed during the Abha airport attack, near the Yemen border, according to Gaca.

Meanwhile, a male resident of Sudanese nationality was killed at King Khalid airport, it added.

The country's civil aviation authority did not name who was responsible for the attacks, but Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said its armed forces had attacked both Saudi Arabia airports with ballistic missiles and drones.

The Houthi military spokesperson also said the Houthis attacked Aden's International Airport in Yemen on Wednesday. The airport is a main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside of Houthi control and has been repeatedly targeted when fighting erupts in the country.

Saree said the two attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports were in "response to the Saudi aggression against our country" which saw "60 airstrikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours".

The civil war in Yemen has worsened in recent weeks, after the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west, seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.

That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping.

But Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have since said they had "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.

They also declared an all out war in an effort to take all territory held by the Houthis.

In a statement issued late on Wednesday, the official spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said the Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports "will not go unpunished".

The spokesperson said the Saudi coalition had targeted more than 80 Houthi military sites across "governorates of Saada, Al Hudaydah, Al Jawf and Ma'rib".

The Saudi-led coalition formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.

A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres has condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting".

Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed on both sides since the latest Houthis' advance.

The UN said on Wednesday more than 200,000 people have been displaced by the escalation.

articles.title: Netanyahu says he brought all the October 7 hostages home. These are the stories of those who didn’t come back alive
articles.summary: Of the 40 hostages who died in captivity, many were killed by their captors while others succumbed to their wounds. Some died in Israeli strikes and operations, while for a few the full circumstances may never be known.
articles.body: The strike plan called for hitting a vast underground complex in Gaza’s southern city of Rafah, comprised of dozens of rooms and a network of interconnecting tunnels. Instead of a dozen bombs, the Israeli military had decided to drop just two munitions, each aimed at a single room. The objective: killing Muhammad Shabaneh, the commander of Hamas’ Rafah Brigade. On May 24, 2024, the bombs hit their marks. But instead of Shabaneh, two Israeli hostages were killed. Two senior Israeli sources said the military had assessed there were no hostages in that part of the complex. Months later, when Israeli ground troops reached the site, they found the bodies of Youssef and Hamza Ziyadne, an Israeli Bedouin father and son who had been kidnapped by Hamas on October 7, 2023. During the deadliest day in the history of the state of Israel, a total of 251 hostages were abducted and taken into Gaza by Hamas-led militants. More than 1,200 people – mostly civilians – were killed in the terror attack. It took two years of war and three ceasefire agreements to return the hostages. Three years later, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insists that he defied the odds and brought all the hostages back home. “We brought back every last one of them,” Netanyahu boasted at the UN General Assembly last month. Facing elections in three weeks, Netanyahu has repeated that statement on multiple occasions, rarely if ever mentioning that not all of the hostages returned home alive. “The fate of every person touches the fibers of our soul, and therefore we invested unceasing effort until we brought back all our hostages, down to the last of them,” he said on Monday, during the official October 7 memorial ceremonies. The Ziyadnes are among 40 hostages taken into Gaza alive who were killed or died in captivity, roughly one in five of the 206 abducted alive. Hamas held them in tunnels and hideaways where, according to released hostages, they were abused, starved, chained and beaten. Many were killed by their captors. Others succumbed to their wounds or the conditions endured in captivity. Some died in Israeli strikes and operations, or in the shadow of Israeli decisions. For a few, the full circumstances may never be known. This account of how those 40 hostages were killed or died in captivity – and why some were not released before their deaths – is based on conversations with dozens of hostage families, as well as Israeli military and government officials who helped piece together their stories. Nearly half were killed by their captors, according to Israeli military officials and forensic evidence reviewed by their families. Among them were 4-year-old Ariel Bibas and his brother, nine-month-old Kfir, who the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said were killed by their captors’ “bare hands,” while 68-year-old Itzhak Elgarat was tortured to death, according to a former hostage and autopsy results. Hamas did not respond to CNN’s request for comment; Palestinian Islamic Jihad said it “does not kill captives.” At least 11 were killed directly by Israeli military fire or in Israeli ground operations: three young men who managed to escape and were shot by troops who mistook them for Palestinian militants, a shooting the IDF Chief of the General Staff concluded should not have been carried out; a 25-year-old named Sahar Baruch who was killed in a failed rescue operation; several hostages who were killed by Israeli bombs. Some of the killings can be linked to nearby Israeli military activity. When the ground offensive began on October 27, 2023, Israeli military officials said Hamas issued a standing order: If Israeli forces approach, move the hostages, and if it’s impossible – kill them. The hostages in Gaza were very aware of the dangers associated with the Israeli military’s presence. Eli Sharabi, who published his firsthand account of captivity in his book “Hostage,” wrote, “That’s what we fear: that IDF commandos will try to enter the tunnel to rescue us by force. Because we know it would never work, and it’d be the end. The end of us. And the end of them.” A CNN review of the circumstances of the 40 hostages’ deaths found that at least 24 – more than half – can be traced back to Israeli military actions, including Israeli strikes and ground maneuvers that led to captors killing their hostages. In every case of a hostage killed by or in proximity to Israeli fire, the military says it had no prior knowledge they were there. The IDF declined to discuss specific cases, citing the privacy of hostage families, but said “all possible measures were taken to avoid putting (the hostages) at risk,” and noted the challenges posed by “a dense and complex civilian environment.” “To the extent that any harm occurred during the complex fighting, it was unintentional and occurred under operational constraints on the ground,” the IDF said in a statement. “The hostages were abducted and held captive by the Hamas terrorist organization, which bore sole responsibility for the conditions of their captivity.” (The Hostages and Missing Families Forum counts 46 living hostages who died in Gaza, but CNN’s investigation found six of those hostages were killed as part of the October 7 attack.) ‘The picture kept shifting’ A few hours after the October 7 attack began, Netanyahu declared unequivocally, “We are at war.” That evening, his cabinet set its main goal – destroying the military and governing capabilities of Hamas and Islamic Jihad. The ensuing three years of war killed more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza, according to the health ministry there. Bringing back the hostages was not part of the original war aims, two Israeli officials said. About a week later, as the scope of abductions became clear, the cabinet added another goal: creating the conditions for their return. The military faced an unprecedented challenge: dense urban combat, some 250 hostages scattered above and below ground and two objectives that appeared to pull in opposite directions. Destroying Hamas would require targeting its leadership. But Hamas, Israeli officials said, kept many hostages close to their senior commanders, using them as “human shields” and making every strike a gamble. The working theory, the officials told CNN, was that most hostages would come home through deals, not rescues, and that military pressure was the only way to bring Hamas to the table. (A total of eight hostages would be rescued in IDF operations.) One senior official called it “synergy.” “The ground maneuver will pressure Hamas to release the hostages, and the more hostages we bring home, the easier it will be to maneuver afterwards,” the official reasoned. But that approach also carried inherent risk for the hostages, some of whom would later be killed by Israeli strikes or gunfire. “We never had 100% intelligence coverage about everyone,” a senior military official said. Hamas constantly moved the captives, so “the picture kept shifting.” Within days of October 7, the military had formed a special hostage task force, led by Maj. Gen. Nitzan Alon. Hundreds of soldiers were assigned to a 24/7 mechanism, linking the air force, intelligence and the IDF’s Southern Command to protect the hostages from Israel’s own offensive. Its main tool was a system of restricted zones around suspected hostage locations, known as “polygons,” drawn broadly at first. These polygons narrowed as intelligence improved; they expanded again after fatal mishaps. Strikes on significant targets, including Hamas military chief Mohammed Deif, and hostage rescue operations, were regularly delayed or called off over concerns for hostage safety, three officials said. Still, as a senior official acknowledged, “It was not without risks and there are places where we failed.” The lost ‘kingdom’ In Khan Younis, the IDF thought it knew where the hostages were. Then, it didn’t. In the first weeks of the war, about 20 hostages were believed to have been held in a huge underground compound, known to the IDF as “the kingdom.” Sources said a polygon had been established there to ensure no Israeli strikes or ground operations endangered the hostages. But after the first ceasefire collapsed in December 2023, the Israeli military launched a major ground offensive in Khan Younis, and the military soon lost track of the hostages. The army believed they had been taken south. It did not know some had been moved to Khan Younis’ northern Hamad City neighborhood. On February 14, 2024, the air force struck a tunnel in that neighborhood, targeting two senior Hamas commanders, unaware of six hostages inside. Only in May did the army grasp what had happened, a military official said. When the bodies were recovered in August, an autopsy found gunshot wounds in all six bodies but could not establish the cause of death. Their captors had also been found dead in the same tunnel, without wounds. Officials believe they were suffocated by the toxins released by the bombs; they cannot rule out the possibility that the hostages were killed by the gases and shot afterwards. Yuval Dancyg, whose father, Alex, was among the dead, says he still doesn’t understand how the army lost track of the hostages in the first place. He said he warned officers in real time that the Khan Younis offensive would kill his father. “They told me not to worry, that they know where he is and they have enough information,” he told CNN. He said the IDF Chief of Staff, Lt. Gen. Herzi Halevi, later acknowledged in a private meeting that the army lacked sufficient information before approving the strike and took responsibility for the fatal error. The army should have been more careful, Dancyg says, but he places most of the blame elsewhere. “The ones that are responsible for what happened to them, first of all, is Hamas,” he said. “But my government could and should have let the hostages out way before. When you have a war with citizens underground and you decide that the war is the most important thing… hostages will get killed.” The price of delay Several senior Israeli officials who were involved in the decision- making have said publicly that more hostages would have come home alive if not for politics. Alon, the general who led the hostage task force, said last week the war “was too long” and could have ended at least a year earlier. Speaking at the Washington Institute, he said Israel could have made the same strategic achievements, and “maybe get some hostages that got killed or murdered during captivity back home alive.” Current and former Israeli officials said Netanyahu frequently stalled progress on the negotiating track and limited his negotiators’ mandate, barring them from discussing an end-of-war deal until the summer of 2025. Dror Shalom, a former senior defense ministry official, said in an interview with Yedioth Ahronoth, “We could have returned dozens of hostages, but because of delays in the process and the rejection of the deals, they simply did not return to us.” The most critical delay, military officials said, came in the spring and summer of 2024. In late May, Netanyahu and his limited security cabinet approved a three-phase proposal that would begin with a six-week ceasefire and the release of 33 elderly and wounded hostages before leading to the release of all others and an end of the war. Then-US President Joe Biden announced the proposal days later, and the United Nations Security Council endorsed it. Hamas took its time answering, two Israeli officials said, but by early July it had signaled it would agree to the May framework, with minor reservations. That’s when Netanyahu decided to harden Israel’s position, military officials said, inserting new demands such as continued Israeli control of the Philadelphi corridor along the Gaza-Egypt border. His security chiefs disagreed, warning the delay could endanger the hostages. The demand had operational and strategic logic, the officials said, but it disrupted what they say was “almost a done deal.” Netanyahu stuck to his new demands. His far-right political allies, Itamar Ben Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, were threatening to withdraw their support and topple the government if Netanyahu moved forward with the deal and ended the war. The Prime Minister’s Office has not responded after CNN reached out multiple times. “There could have been a deal in July,” said Oren Setter, a retired IDF brigadier general who served as deputy director for strategy and negotiations at the Hostages Taskforce. “Hamas was under a lot of pressure and was willing to negotiate with flexibility,” he told CNN. “The fact that we stayed on that Philadelphi issue for so long lost us the opportunity.” “We knew that the price could be the life of the hostages,” he added. A few weeks later, that price had names. The ‘Beautiful Six’ By August 2024, Israeli troops had spent months advancing through Rafah and were concentrating on the tunnels under the Tel Al-Sultan neighborhood, where Hamas commanders were believed to be hiding. There was no concrete intelligence of hostages in the area, two officials said, and the IDF’s subsequent investigation put the likelihood of hostages being there as “medium to low.” On August 27, troops found a Bedouin Israeli hostage, Farhan Al-Qadi, alone in a tunnel. He reported recently hearing a woman speaking Hebrew nearby, saying “good morning.” After a 24-hour pause in operations, Israeli troops pressed on in the tunnel system. On August 31, soldiers found six bodies in a tunnel just a few hundred meters away. They had been shot, likely two days earlier, the IDF said. The army’s official investigation concluded they were murdered by their captors, and that the Israeli maneuver, “although gradual and cautious, had a circumstantial influence” on their execution. Officials say five of the six were slated for release under the May framework, had it been agreed to. One was Hersh Goldberg-Polin, a 23-year-old Israeli-American citizen kidnapped from the Nova music festival. His mother, Rachel, declines to assign blame. “Pointing fingers does not bring Hersh back, and does not ease my pain,” she said. The bodies of the six, she told CNN, came back skeletal and filthy. They had been starved and tortured. Widely known as the “Beautiful Six,” they were the last hostages to die in captivity. Israeli officials say that by then, the working methods and intelligence coverage had dramatically improved. But the war went on for more than a year. The deadlock broke briefly after US President Donald Trump’s reelection: in January 2025, a three-phase ceasefire took effect. Its terms were nearly identical to the deal that was on the verge of being approved the previous summer. Over the ceasefire’s first six weeks, 30 living hostages and eight deceased were released. Then the truce collapsed and Israel went back to war. The last 20 living hostages walked free on October 13, 2025 under Trump’s 20-point peace plan. On January 26, 2026, Israel recovered the remains of the last deceased Israeli hostage, Ran Gvili, and the count was complete. But when political leaders say they brought all the hostages home, Rachel Goldberg-Polin asks them to stop. “Please don’t say that you brought him home… Hersh is buried in the ground five miles from my home, but Hersh never came back to my home.”

articles.title: UK bluefin tuna comeback shows nature can recover, says WWF
articles.summary: The tuna is one of several wildlife recoveries highlighted in a major new report from WWF.
articles.body:
Bluefin tuna have returned in huge numbers off the British coast after almost disappearing from UK waters.

The return of the giant predatory fish is one of several wildlife recoveries highlighted in a major new report from WWF, which it says shows conservation can work.

However, the Living Planet Report 2026 also found that monitored wildlife populations around the world have fallen by an average of 73% since 1970.

The wildlife conservation charity said nature remains in "freefall" but it called the report one of hope.

"It's not too late," Mike Barrett, chief scientific adviser at WWF-UK, told the BBC.

Restored wetland becomes haven for rare birds

Five endangered African birds hatch at Chester Zoo

The UK was once home to large tuna fisheries, but overfishing of both the tuna and the smaller fish it preys on meant that by the 1960s it had largely disappeared.

The report credits its recent recovery to a concerted international effort that included reducing catch quotas, size limits and protection of spawning grounds, which was backed by campaigns from consumers, chefs and retailers.

Hannah Rudd, head of marine at the Angling Trust, said the result of this effort was close to an "explosion" in the population of the species.

"I think bluefin tuna is a golden case study that fisheries management works," she said.

The WWF report highlighted other species recoveries around the world, including an increase of more than 70% in the number of wild tigers - from around 3,200 in 2010 to about 5,700 in 2025.

Last year, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle to have its protection status downgraded from "endangered" to "least concern", after 50 years of conservation work in about 80 countries.

Elephant numbers are stable or growing in parts of southern Africa, thanks in part to new laws that give local people a share of the income elephants bring, including tourism.

Barrett said these successes resulted from a clear goal with a credible plan and people who believed they could make a difference. The report calls it "the science of hope".

"Hope is not the same thing as wishful thinking," he said. "Hope is not passive. Hope's about action."

But despite the individual successes, the overall picture for nature remains stark.

Working with the Zoological Society of London, WWF tracks nearly 36,000 populations of almost 6,000 species of mammals, birds, fish, reptiles and amphibians.

It estimates global monitored wildlife populations have fallen by an average of 73% since 1970.

The figure measures the average change in the size of those populations, not the number of animals lost. About half of the populations are stable or growing, but their gains are outweighed by losses elsewhere.

Dr Katie Collins, a senior curator at the Natural History Museum in London, also said the index misses out vast numbers of important species because it covers only vertebrates, missing plants, insects and other creatures they depend on.

"If you lose garden snails, you lose the song thrush," she warned.

WWF says conservation alone cannot reverse the decline but there must be efforts to tackle the causes.

The biggest pressures come from farming, which can destroy the habitats wildlife depends on, and burning fossil fuels for energy, which drives climate change.

The organisation says the money is flowing the wrong way. In 2023, about $7.3 trillion (£5.53tn) went into activities that harm nature, compared with $220bn spent protecting or restoring it, the report estimates – a ratio of roughly 33 to one.

Barrett has worked on seven Living Planet reports, but he said this was the first where the takeaway message was to focus on hope.

"The fact that the science is still telling us that we've got a way out is actually extraordinary," he said.

"So it's a closing window of opportunity, but it's still open, just, if we act now."

Additional reporting Kevin Church and Miho Tanaka

articles.title: Syrian general accused of atrocities paid and protected by US and Lebanon, BBC finds
articles.summary: Bassam al-Hassan, linked to reporter Austin Tice's abduction, is being sheltered in return for information.
articles.body:
A former Syrian general wanted for crimes against humanity is being bankrolled and protected by the US and Lebanese authorities, a BBC News investigation has found.

Bassam al-Hassan, who oversaw Syria's chemical weapons programme and was a senior adviser to former President Bashar al-Assad, is being harboured in Lebanon following the Assad regime's collapse in 2024.

An investigation by the BBC and the US broadcaster NPR has discovered that Hassan has been allowed to remain there under an arrangement involving the FBI, and other US and Lebanese authorities. This is because of his willingness to provide information about the abduction of American journalist Austin Tice in Syria in 2012, as well as additional intelligence, we have been told.

Last month the BBC revealed Tice's abduction had been a planned operation , with Hassan in the chain of command.

Officials from two different branches of Syria's new government have told the BBC they want Hassan returned to face trial, but that US authorities want him kept in Lebanon, and they say there is little Damascus can do about this.

We asked the FBI, the CIA and Lebanon's General Directorate of General Security to comment on our findings. Only the FBI responded, declining to comment and instead directing us to a past statement that said its focus remained on establishing the facts around the Tice case and securing his return.

In response to our findings, Phil Elwood, spokesperson for the Tice family said: "If what you are saying is true, the fact that our tax dollars are being used to furnish a comfortable life for someone associated with the use of chemical weapons on Syrian civilians, who claims to have had Austin Tice executed, is offensive.

"This is nothing less than aiding and abetting the escape of a wanted war criminal. The Syrians deserve justice and he should be returned to stand trial."

As part of a years-long investigation featured in the new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? Series 3 of I'm Not A Monster Presents, the BBC has reviewed a detailed record of a meeting between Hassan, FBI and CIA representatives, and Lebanese security officials, where Tice's case is discussed.

In it, Hassan is offered "residency", "protection" and help securing his "living needs" in return for information, primarily about Tice.

Sources with knowledge of the arrangement confirmed this was the case, and described to us how Hassan receives money from the US authorities through an intermediary, making it harder to trace. Hassan is sanctioned by the US government.

Yet people connected to the Tice investigation say they have seen little evidence it has significantly advanced since Hassan began providing information as part of this agreement. The deal is believed to have been struck in the spring of 2025.

Sources with knowledge of the investigation have expressed concerns that Hassan's arrangement with the US could continue indefinitely, at significant expense but with little gain.

Hassan is not the only Syrian regime official whose connection to the Tice case has seemingly afforded him financial payments or assistance for living abroad.

One former regime member said he had received money from the FBI multiple times in exchange for his co-operation on Tice's case. It was "not in his interest to share all the information all at once," he told the BBC, "in order to be able to drag out how long he can continue to receive payments from them [the US authorities]".

Another former regime member connected to the Tice case claimed he was living in Lebanon under the "patronage" of the US authorities, citing this as the reason he could not speak to us about Tice.

The BBC spoke to a former senior Lebanese intelligence official who confirmed that Lebanese intelligence does have arrangements with the Americans, and that these types of payments have and do take place when both agencies have overlap in cases, but said he had no knowledge of payments involving the Tice case.

Following the fall of the Assad regime in early December 2024, Hassan is believed to have initially escaped to Iran.

A Syrian businessman, with strong connections to both the former regime and the Lebanese authorities, told the BBC that negotiations had then taken place - involving the US, Lebanon, and Iran - to bring Hassan to Lebanon.

The businessman, who asked to remain anonymous, said Hassan was valuable, not only because of what he is believed to know about Tice, but because of his knowledge of Syria's chemical weapons programme and its military relationship with Iran - secrets that US intelligence was allegedly interested in.

Hassan told US investigators last year that Tice had been executed on former President Assad's orders, but several people with knowledge of the investigation have questioned the details of his account. Hassan has provided a potential location for Tice's remains, but when the site was searched, nothing was found - according to multiple sources familiar with the dig - casting doubt on the validity of some of Hassan's information.

There are questions, however, over how thoroughly the site was searched. Two sources who said they had intimate knowledge of the operation told the BBC that US authorities stopped digging before the search had been completed, possibly because of security concerns.

When the BBC managed to reach Hassan by phone last year to ask for an interview, he directed us to seek permission for him to speak from the FBI and CIA at the US embassy in Beirut.

Our investigation has found that other Syrian officials connected to the Tice case have also apparently found refuge abroad.

They include Mohammad Makhlouf, who reported to Hassan in Syria and was connected to Tice's detention - now believed to be residing in Lebanon. And Sakr Rustom, Hassan's nephew who was involved in Tice's abduction, now believed to be moving between the UAE and Lebanon. When the BBC attempted to speak to Rustom about Tice's case, he said he "preferred to focus on matters of the future".

Ghassan Nassour, a former general in Syria's Republican Guard, is said by former members of the National Defence Forces to have presided over the jail Tice was held in, and is believed to be living in the UAE with his family, we have been told.

articles.title: Bourne Woods ranger retires after 'remarkable' 38 years
articles.summary: William McLaughlin leaves a "lasting legacy" of care at Bourne Woods in Lincolnshire, bosses say.
articles.body:
A "passionate" woodsman who spent almost four decades caring for wildlife has retired.

William McLaughlin spent 37 years working as Forestry England wildlife ranger at Bourne Woods, in Lincolnshire.

The 68-year-old, who was responsible for conservation and deer management, said: "If your job is your hobby, you don't work a day in your life."

Scott Martin, Forestry England manager for Bourne Woods, said: "His passion, expertise and dedication have made a lasting difference to these forests and the wildlife that depends on them."

McLaughlin said his love of the outdoors stemmed from childhood.

"I just always loved being in the woods," he said. "It was my environment."

He moved to Lincolnshire in 1990 after spending 15 years as a gamekeeper in Scotland's Western Isles.

"I couldn't think of anything else I would have done.

"The wood is alive – why would you want to be anywhere else?"

Reflecting on his career, McLaughlin said: "I've traveled in the London underground, people do that daily, all their working lives, and I think why would anyone want to do that?

"My favourite thing is being out here in the woods."

Deer management was an "integral" part of his role.

"If you have an unmanaged deer population, they pretty much destroy it, grazing on young vegetation meaning trees can't grow, which has a knock-on effect to wildlife."

Martin said McLaughlin's "wealth of knowledge" had been invaluable in "helping us care for these special places".

"His work on deer management has played a vital role in supporting the natural regeneration of native tree species, while his collaboration with local conservation groups has helped deliver positive outcomes for wildlife across the area.

"His contribution leaves a lasting legacy and we thank him for his remarkable service and wish him a long, happy and well-deserved retirement."

Despite retiring, McLaughlin said he would remain a familiar face in the woods.

"I won't miss it, because I'm still going to be here. I will miss my colleagues and the friends I have made though."

articles.title: Signage at UK consulate in East Jerusalem removed as Israel’s deadline over
articles.summary: Thursday marks 30 days since Israel’s foreign minister ordered the closure of the UK consulate in occupied East Jerusalem.
articles.body:
Workers at the UK consulate in occupied East Jerusalem have removed its signage as the Israeli shutdown deadline arrives, further damaging strained ties between allies.

Journalists from the Reuters news agency saw ‌workers remove a plaque reading “British Consulate General” from the building on Thursday, as well as another sign for its consular section. The UK flag was still flying over the building.

Thursday marks 30 days since Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar ordered the closure of the consulate in occupied East Jerusalem. The move was in response to the UK’s wave of sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements, including a ban on importing goods made there.

The United Nations and most countries consider the settlements illegal under international law. Israel disputes this.

The United Kingdom threatened to expel 27 Israeli diplomats if Israel proceeded to close the consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, according to unverified Israeli media reports.

The consulate has not responded to an immediate request for comment.

Israel has been adamant the consulate will close even as the UK has sought to keep it open, including sending the country’s top national security adviser to Israel last week for talks.

The UK’s presence in the city dates back almost 200 years, long before the state of Israel was established in 1948. The closure order does not affect the UK’s embassy in Tel Aviv, which handles diplomatic relations with Israel’s government.

The consulate, in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of occupied East Jerusalem, handles the UK’s relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem, as well as in ‌the occupied West ⁠Bank and Gaza. It also provides consular services to Palestinians.

The UK Foreign Office on Wednesday declined to comment when asked whether the consulate was still operating or if diplomats working there had returned to the UK.

Despite the current strains, the ⁠UK and Israel are close economic, security and intelligence partners.

articles.title: Protesters in Colombia rally against ties with Israel
articles.summary: Hundreds took to the streets of Bogota to protest against the ongoing genocide in Gaza.
articles.body:
Protesters have rallied in Colombia’s capital opposing the new far-right government’s policy towards Israel.

Hundreds took to the streets of Bogota on Wednesday to protest against the ongoing genocide in Gaza and the Colombian government’s decision to restore diplomatic and economic relations with Israel.

The protesters, who began their rally in front of the Israeli embassy in Bogota, criticised President Abelardo de la Espriella’s decision to open a new Colombian embassy in Jerusalem.

The rally marked three years since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, which were followed by Israel launching a genocidal war on Gaza.

“When diplomatic relations with Israel were broken off, the message was that we would not be a nation complicit in their atrocities,” Nicolas Isaza, who took part in the protest, told Al Jazeera.

“Today our government is no longer drawing a line against the atrocities being committed in Palestine,” he added.

De la Espriella, who was sworn in as president in August, promised close relations with the US and Israel during his election campaign as a way to combat armed groups in his country.

Colombia’s government has since restored relations with Israel after former President Gustavo Petro, who criticised Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, severed diplomatic relations and halted Israeli arms imports.

The Colombian government also recognised Israel’s claim of sovereignty over the occupied Syrian Golan Heights, just days after the new president took power.

articles.title: 'Arrogant' SpaceXAI does not attend Suffolk MP's NYC testimony
articles.summary: Lowestoft MP Jess Asato gives evidence to a New York hearing as the city vows to regulate AI developers.
articles.body:
A Suffolk MP has been giving evidence to New York City Council as it becomes the first American body to put forward laws to regulate AI developers.

Jess Asato is suing xAI in the UK after sexualised images of her were created by its AI chatbot tool, Grok.

She is seeking damages from the company, owned by Elon Musk, for the misuse of her private information and breaches of data protection rules.

Asato told the BBC that the failure of SpaceXAI - which owns xAI - to turn up at the hearing, despite being subpoenaed, demonstrated its "level of arrogance". SpaceXAI has been contacted for comment.

The hearing, which was held on 5 October, was the council's Committee of the Whole - a rare meeting where all council members are present.

In her opening statement, the speaker, Julie Menin, acknowledged the benefit of AI use on science and medical breakthroughs, but said the meeting had been called in response to "serious existential safety concerns" over AI development and "the catastrophic dangers of the technology".

She added that the lack of federal regulation of AI developers in the USA had meant they needed to develop effective AI regulation in New York.

In America, national laws are made by federal government - but states and cities can also make their own legislation.

After being invited to speak about her experiences and legal action, Asato said: "It was quite a long way to go but I thought if I could take the message of what we're trying to do here in the UK over to New York, to the centre of AI and tech development, then I might be able to help to get a much safer platform built for the future."

She said her flight and accommodation had been paid for by Reset Tech, a public policy organisation advocating for technology that protects children, consumers, and public safety.

Asato filed a lawsuit back in July , suing xAI for damages after non-consensual images and videos, including some showing her being sexually assaulted, were shared online.

She is seeking damages for the misuse of her private information and breaches of data protection rules, as well as a court order requiring the company to find and remove any remaining online images.

xAI is yet to file a defence to the legal action.

Asato said she also highlighted in her evidence that women were disproportionally affected.

She said: "We know that 99% of images that are made into sexualised videos are of women. 90% of deep fake pornographic images are of women, so it's a very gendered crime.

"They also specifically asked me about elected representatives, because obviously I am a member of parliament, and I talked about the fact that we also know that women are 33 times more likely to be targeted by sexual deep fakes than men who are elected.

"So it is definitely something that we can see right across the piece, whether you're elected or not. Women are targeted by deep fake AI."

At the hearing, the five major AI developers in New York - Anthropic, Meta, Google, OpenAI and SpaceXAI - were subpoenaed to testify.

Four of them turned up but SpaceXAI did not send a representative.

Asato said: "I think it shows a certain amount of arrogance or a sense that actually these companies don't need to be held accountable by elected representatives."

Menin told the hearing the city would be pursuing SpaceXAI through the courts as its no-show was a "direct violation".

articles.title: A Nova Scotia man lost his wallet as a teenager in 1975; 51 years later, a carpenter found it under floorboards with his birth certificate, student ID, $1 bill and a Hamlet ticket still inside
articles.summary: A wallet lost by a teenager in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, in 1975 has been returned to its owner 51 years later after a carpenter discovered it hidden under
articles.body: A wallet lost by a teenager in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, in 1975 has been returned to its owner 51 years later after a carpenter discovered it hidden under floorboards during a home renovation. The brown leather wallet still contained a birth certificate, a student ID, a one-dollar bill and a ticket stub for a production of Hamlet, all preserved beneath the old flooring. Local news and national outlets like UPI.com and PEOPLE reported that the wallet’s owner, now in his 60s, was reunited with the long-lost item after the carpenter tracked him down through the documents inside. Read more details about it, as per the reports, here:A wallet slipped away in the mid-1970sCarpenter Matty Goldsmith, who was working on a house in Dartmouth, in Nova Scotia, Canada, found wallet under the house’s old floors. Seeing the ID documents, like a driver’s license, birth certificate, and a 1975 theater ticket for Hamlet among other things made Goldsmith think about trying his luck in finding its owner now, reported Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC). Afterall, the find was more than a curiosity. It was a time capsule from a specific moment in the life of a Dartmouth resident, preserved almost by accident!Through the documents, Goldsmith found out that the wallet originally belonged to Richard Gilroy, who was a Dartmouth teenager roughly about 17 years old in 1975. He assumed that maybe Gilroy was working as a construction worker at the site and hence might have lost his wallet under the old floors. considering how the world has shrunk with the internet, carpenter Goldsmith and his colleagues thought of posting about this finding on a local Facebook group to find out the original owner of the old wallet, as per reports.Tracking down the owner after 51 yearsAs per PEOPLE, on September 23, Goldsmith posted a photo of Gilroy’s student ID along with the caption, “Anyone know a Richard Gilroy born 1958 who went to Dartmouth High in 1975? I found his wallet during a renovation that’s been lost in the walls since 1975! Lots of neat treasure in it, would love to get it back to him if possible!” And surprisingly, Gilroy’s wife, Donna, commented on the post saying that it was her husband's, who is “alive and well”, and he does remember losing the wallet more than 50 years ago!On September 26, carpenter Goldsmith replied to Gilroy's wife, Donna, and told her that he'll be returning the wallet. articles.title: Maidenhead council 'extremely concerned' by Travelodge report
articles.summary: Findings will be raised with South Oxfordshire District Council where Travelodge's HQ is based.
articles.body:
The issues raised by an independent report into the sexual assault of a woman in a Travelodge will be raised by an "extremely concerned" council.

The attack happened in December 2022 at the Maidenhead branch when a man lied to hotel staff to obtain a key card for the woman's room in the early hours.

The report published last week found the Thame-based company failed the victim at every stage of the process and guests are still not being kept "as safe as they should be".

Travelodge previously apologised and said: "Guest safety remains a top priority and this work will build on the large-scale programme of change."

Listen to the latest news from Berkshire

Local authorities have the power to enforce health and safety legislation by inspecting hotels and, under licensing laws, they can also review a hotel's license to operate.

A spokesperson for Royal Borough of Windsor and Maidenhead said: "We take the issues raised by this incident extremely seriously and will be discussing the findings of the independent report with South Oxfordshire District Council, who are Travelodge's primary authority, in line with our responsibilities for enforcing health and safety legislation.

"We'll also consider any relevant implications through our Community Safety Partnership, including our work to tackle violence against women and girls."

The UK headquarters of Travelodge is in Thame, Oxfordshire.

South Oxfordshire District Council has been contacted for a response.

Speaking when the report was published, the company said "Travelodge unreservedly apologises again to the woman assaulted" adding that "guest safety remains a top priority and this work will build on the large-scale programme of change".

articles.title: Why single Ebola death in Kenya has sparked fears of wider African spread
articles.summary: According to the WHO, the Kenyan patient first got sick in the DRC, where the patient had been living, and was treated there.
articles.body:
Kenya reported its first death from a deadly strain of Ebola virus which had spread widely, starting in the Democratic Republic of Congo earlier this year.

The Bundibugyo (BDBV) strain of Ebola was first detected in Uganda in 2007, according to the WHO. The ongoing outbreak in the DRC has killed at least 4,148 people out of 8,300 reported cases. It also spread across the border to Uganda, which had about 20 cases before being declared Ebola-free in July.

However, the person who died in Kenya from the disease had travelled from the DRC to Uganda over land before taking a flight to Nairobi, raising questions about Uganda’s status as “Ebola-free”, concerns about the rigidity of Kenya’s screening processes for people coming into the country and fears it may have spread further than previously thought.

On Tuesday, the World Health Organization said the Kenyan government is now enhancing its disease surveillance with more targeted screening at high-risk points of entry.

But Wolfgang Preiser, a professor and head of medical virology at Stellenbosch University in South Africa, explained that while efforts are being made to bring the outbreak under control, it has grown so much that “sheer numbers and the speed of spread are overwhelming for many systems.”

“I am not surprised that cases have reached other provinces in DRC and neighbouring countries. I expect that this will continue to happen until such time that the trajectory has been reversed and case numbers are in decline,” he told Al Jazeera.

It is a serious, potentially deadly viral infection which can be caught when a person comes into contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person or wild animal, including fluid lingering on surfaces. People have also been known to contract the disease through eating contaminated meat.

There have been many outbreaks in Central, West and East Africa.

A West African outbreak from 2014 to 2016 killed at least 11,300 people of a reported 28,600 cases and accelerated the push to develop a vaccine. That was a different strain of the Ebola virus, known as Zaire, for which there is now a vaccine.

The strain behind the latest outbreak is Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), which is believed to have been caused by a new transmission from animals to humans, before then spreading between humans, rather than by variants linked to earlier outbreaks. There is no vaccine for Bundibugyo.

Symptoms can appear between two and 21 days after infection and can start suddenly with flu-like symptoms, including a high temperature, fatigue, and a headache. It can lead to internal and external bleeding, impaired liver and kidney function and organ failure.

Kenyan Health Minister Aden Duale told reporters that the Kenyan patient, who has not been named, first became sick one month ago in the DRC, where they had been living for several years, and was treated there.

On October 2, the patient travelled by road to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, via Beni, then flew to Nairobi, arriving the next day.

After he arrived at the airport in Kenya, a relative and a friend took him to a hospital, where he was quickly isolated, and tests showed he had the virus, Duale said. Despite receiving care, the patient died from the virus on Monday and was buried on Tuesday in line with the country’s Ebola protocol.

So far, health authorities in Kenya have identified 28 potential contacts, including family members and health workers who cared for the infected patient. Authorities are also separately tracking 23 passengers and four crew members from his flight, “with arrangements underway for appropriate follow-up and quarantine of people assessed to be at risk”, the WHO reported.

Jean Bisimwa Nachenga, a professor in infectious diseases at Stellenbosch University, emphasised that the virus does not “respect national borders.”

“Population mobility, displacement, cross-border trade, and fragile healthcare systems make containment particularly challenging. In eastern DRC, ongoing insecurity further complicates surveillance, contact tracing, and access to affected communities,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Regional cooperation is therefore essential.”

How did a sick patient get past screening in both Uganda and Kenya?

Passengers travelling to, from or through Uganda and Kenya have to pass multiple airport temperature checks and complete at least two digital forms intended to flag any potential exposure to the virus in the DRC. Somehow, the infected person in this case was missed by these checks.

Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja said Kampala was not to blame for the Kenyan man catching the virus and wrote on X, “Leave Uganda out of this conversation. We don’t have Ebola here.”

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the Ugandan Ministry of Health said the man had a “normal temperature” when he was screened at the Entebbe airport before his departure.

Kenyan authorities say he may have taken medication to mask his symptoms when he was later screened at Nairobi airport. Investigations are continuing, however.

“We are trying to retrieve the digital form he would have filled out at Entebbe airport when he went through the thermal scanning process to see what he declared in that form. The form includes questions about recent health problems but also whether a traveller was recently in DRC,” Richard Mugahi, a senior Ugandan health official, told the Reuters news agency.

“We are also going through airport security camera footage to see if we can identify the driver who dropped him at the airport so we can trace any contacts here.”

Preiser also said the tracking system “seems to work as it did in Uganda,” with a diagnosis made rapidly as soon as the patient sought care in Kenya.

“It will be instructive to try and trace back what happened at the various stops during his travels, and lessons should be heeded by all countries,” he said.

He cited an example from a previous Ebola outbreak in West Africa, when a “British nurse fell sick during her return trip to the UK and reported to the medical check in Heathrow, only to be sent onwards to her destination where she was diagnosed with Ebola”.

The lesson, he said was that “even cooperative travellers and good systems may fall through the net”.

Since it began in the DRC’s northeastern Ituri province, the latest outbreak has spread this year to seven provinces in the country’s north and east. It was officially declared an outbreak in the DRC in May.

Weak infrastructure, the remoteness of the region in eastern DRC, and ongoing conflict with armed groups near the borders with South Sudan, Uganda, and Rwanda have hindered efforts to respond to cases quickly and effectively.

The response to the outbreak has been further complicated by several factors, including strikes by unpaid health workers, misinformation and cultural traditions. These have included open-casket family burials of some of those killed by the virus earlier on during the outbreak, potentially increasing the risk of further transmission.

The United Nations reported on Friday last week that an Ebola-hit camp housing a transit centre for infected patients was burned by soldiers earlier this week when they were looking for weapons on the outskirts of Bunia, the capital city of Ituri province, which is at the epicentre of the outbreak.

The incident forced 19,000 people to flee the camp.

The disease also spread to Uganda, where 20 people who had travelled from DRC were treated before the country declared it was free of Ebola in July.

Recently, it has become increasingly hard to contain within DRC.

On Monday, Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, warned that there had been an “alarming surge” of cases in eastern North Kivu province, which borders Uganda, and where 40 percent of all new cases are currently being recorded.

“It is like fighting a megafire,” Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator at MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in the city of Butembo, said. “Multiple outbreaks are developing at the same time, with varying intensity and in different locations.”

Some 2 million people live in North Kivu’s city of Butembo and surrounding areas, but it has only four Ebola treatment centres, two of which opened recently, MSF told the media. Patients often have to be transferred elsewhere, increasing the risk of infection to others, Hoffman said.

The WHO is working with Kenyan authorities to trace contacts and to strengthen checks for travellers coming into the country.

Mohamed Janabi, WHO regional director for Africa, said on Tuesday that “health emergency preparedness gives us a head start”.

“Kenya has put important outbreak control measures in place. The priority now is to move swiftly to detect any further cases before the virus has an opportunity to spread. We’re supporting the ongoing efforts to strengthen the response, and with rapid and coordinated action, we can prevent the virus from gaining a foothold and stop a potential larger outbreak,” Janabi said.

The agency also said it has delivered about 1,000 Ebola tests and “1,000 personal protective equipment kits to high-risk counties in Kenya”.

In June, the Kenyan government granted the United States permission to set up an Ebola quarantine facility at the Laikipia airbase, 120 miles (193km) from the capital, Nairobi, to treat infected Americans travelling from African nations before they arrived in the US. The scheme generated uproar from locals who feared transmission of the disease, and Kenyan courts halted the plan.

Overall, Nachenga said that merely strengthening border screening wasn’t enough. It was also important to “reinforce the entire public health response”.

“This means training frontline healthcare workers, ensuring rapid laboratory diagnosis, promptly isolating suspected cases, and tracing and monitoring contacts. Kenya’s ability to identify this case provides an important opportunity to strengthen preparedness,” he added.

articles.title: Why hot summer could lead to smaller potatoes in supermarkets
articles.summary: Farmers say yields are down because they have had to harvest smaller potatoes earlier than normal.
articles.body:
As the roller shutter door opens to reveal one of Tim Rooke's potato stores, the harvest looks impressive. Seven hundred tonnes are kept in this building alone, ready to be turned into crisps.

Yet North Yorkshire farmer Rooke is far from happy. He plucks a large potato from the pile and in his other hand, places two much smaller ones.

"We've probably lost two tonnes on every fifty tonnes in here, potatoes that have just fallen through the graders because they are far too small."

The prolonged dry spell this summer meant his crop was beginning to die. He was forced to harvest early, but that meant his potatoes hadn't grown to the size his customers want.

"There will be fewer potatoes grown going forward. They are a very expensive crop to grow," says Tim when the BBC visits his farm near Helmsley.

"There's less enthusiasm to have the expense of growing that crop when we have some sort of climate change hitting us year after year after year. We're nearly getting to the stage where enough is enough.

"Most potatoes require 200ml of rain or other water and this year they've had about 35ml. It's also been incredibly warm. Potatoes don't bulk up above 28°C. I think we've had 40 days above that."

It's a similar story of falling crop yields near Selby, where farmer Richard Bramley would like the government to provide interest-free loans to farmers so they can invest.

"We think our potatoes will be 20 to 25% down," he says.

"We have to generate the income not just to live, but to produce the following year's crop. That's the dilemma so many farmers find themselves in a the moment.

"Off the back of two, maybe three really bad years, the resilience in the farming industry is starting to break down. I think we certainly have a problem, quite when it will really manifest itself I am not entirely sure."

A statement from the Department of the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA) confirmed the issue is on Andy Burnham's desk.

"Food security is national security and one of the Prime Minister's first visits was meeting farmers hit by drought and dry weather, announcing a £65m package."

It added: "We're going further to address the risks of climate change and nature loss - including a new taskforce to strengthen climate security."

Scott Walker, chief executive of growers' association GB Potatoes, said shoppers should expect fewer large varieties of potato on the shelves this year.

"The prolonged hot and dry weather placed significant pressure on the British crop and has restricted the growth of potatoes. With harvesting still under way, we will not know the full impact until the crop has been lifted, but as well as fewer potatoes there will be fewer large potatoes this year.

"Consumers are likely to notice this most with baking potatoes, where the sizes available will be smaller than usual.

"The supply chain is extremely good at making the best use of the crop that is available, so consumers will continue to find good quality potatoes and potato products that are good value for money."

Back in Helmsley, Tim Rooke wants changes to planning laws to make it easier to build and run water storage lagoons, capturing winter rain and using it in the summer.

"We need a more relaxed attitude to allow this to happen.

"This is our third bad harvest in five. The weather has certainly altered in this area. We have to adapt and it's time we started or we're going to end with not many potato farmers left in this country."

articles.title: US has lost or sustained damage to 81 military aircraft worth up to $3.3 billion in Iran war, congressional report says
articles.summary: That’s almost double the 42 aircraft the non-partisan agency counted in a report released six months ago.
articles.body: The United States military has had 81 aircraft destroyed or damaged in the war with Iran, a Congressional Research Service report released this week says. The number includes both airplanes and helicopters as well as drones, with the MQ-9 Reaper drone – used for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, close air support and combat search and rescue – accounting for more than half of the losses. But also on the list are some of the Pentagon’s most-prized assets, including an F-35A fighter jet and an E-3 Sentry, the four-engine jet with a large radar dome atop the fuselage used for target tracking and airspace management. The total cost of the aircraft lost is between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion, depending on the Defense Department’s plans for replacements, the report said, citing figures from the Congressional Budget Office. The total cost of the war is much higher – at least $45 billion, sources have told CNN. That figure doesn’t include damage to infrastructure at US bases in the region, including those where some of the aircraft losses happened. Some of the aircraft included in the count may have been returned to service, including eight F-15 Strike Eagle fighter jets that sustained light damage in an Iranian strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, Jordan, in September. The report is based on numbers contained in statements from the Defense Department; its inspector general; US Central Command, which has been conducting the operations against Iran; and news reports reviewed by the CRS. The report poses several questions for congressional consideration, including whether lawmakers are getting enough information from the Pentagon on the losses to determine effects and remedies. Defense Department reporting on Iran war losses has, to date, been vague. Even the Pentagon inspector general’s report on the losses, released in September, and covering action from February 28 to June 30, cites previous CRS reports for some of its aircraft loss numbers. Other issues Congress needs to think about are whether to provide funding for repairs or replacements; whether there is enough industrial capacity to satisfy those requirements; and the effects on US military sales to foreign partners. It also raises questions about how the Iran war has affected US posture outside the Middle East. “Congress may assess whether losses in certain high-demand platforms that are aging and limited in number, such as the E-3 Sentry, create capability gaps or increase risk in other theaters,” the report says. Analysts have said actions in the Middle East, including the Iran war and earlier confrontations with the Houthi rebels in Yemen, an Iranian proxy group, have taken an especially heavy toll on the MQ-9 drones, which Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach told Congress earlier this year was the military’s “most valuable player” in the war with Iran. Forty-five have been lost in the Middle East this year, “an alarming rate,” according to a September report from the Atlantic Council. The Air Force has lost about 35% of its MQ-9s since 2004, it says.
